blocks.text: This is perhaps the most famous and industrially significant process. The "Dow Process" (or variations of it) is a multi-step chemical and electrochemical process used to extract magnesium metal from the vast reserves of magnesium ions (Mg²⁺) present in seawater.
Seawater is treated with calcium hydroxide (Ca(OH)₂), derived from limestone or oyster shells), which precipitates magnesium as insoluble magnesium hydroxide (Mg(OH)₂).
Magnesium hydroxide is filtered and then reacted with hydrochloric acid (HCl) to form magnesium chloride (MgCl₂).

The magnesium chloride solution is then concentrated and dried. The molten MgCl₂ is subjected to electrolysis in large electrolytic cells. This is the final step that produces pure magnesium metal at the cathode and chlorine gas at the anode.

This process is famous for its ingenuity in extracting a valuable metal from an abundant, low-concentration source (sea water) on a massive industrial scale. It has revolutionized the magnesium production.
